newsitem.title: USA: Core U.S. CPI above forecasts but trend still tame.
newsitem.headline: Core U.S. CPI above forecasts but trend still tame.

text.p: April U.S. consumer price growth, excluding weak food and energy prices, edged above Wall Street's expectations but economists said the underlying trend remains soft and should not alarm Federal Reserve policymakers.

"I don't think it is the straw that breaks their back one way or the other. I still think you are dealing with a 50/50 chance that (the Fed) could move on Tuesday," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.
Fed policymakers meet May 20 to decide monetary policy.
Sending U.S. Treasuries shooting lower just after the price data release was an unexpected fall in U.S. weekly jobless claims, which played on market fears of worrisome labor market tightness.
"I think the claims number is what's driving the (Treasury) market in here," said Nancy Kimelman, chief economist at Technical Data in Boston.
The Labor Department reported that the U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.1 percent in April while the core CPI, the index without its more volatile food and energy components, rose 0.3 percent.
The overall CPI hit Wall Street's target but the core rate had been expected to rise only 0.2 percent, according to a Reuters poll.

Economists said Fed decision makers are not likely to be swayed much by the CPI data, as the trend in core CPI growth still averages about 0.2 percent. The FOMC meets next week to decide whether to raise U.S. interest rates for a second time this year.

"I don't think the Fed is going to get too excited about the CPI. The underlying trend in inflation is still soft and a slightly above-trend figure is not going to create any panic," said David Sloan, senior economist at I.D.E.A. consultancy.
However, the data did slightly tarnish the rosy inflation outlook depicted in Wednesday's April producer price index, which fell an unexpected 0.6 percent.

"PPI was very favorable and this is a mild negative. I don't think this will change people's view of what the Fed will do," said Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc, who added he expects the Fed will hold rates steady next week.
Apparel, airline and tobacco prices were the big gainers in the April CPI report. Energy and food/beverage costs dropped as had been expected.
